clue.text: Isherwood-inspired piece involving bearcat

indicators.note: involving in its sense of entangling or mixing up, so the letters of the following word are jumbled together

explanation.surface: A stage work drawn from Isherwood happens to feature an odd animal, the bearcat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involving' looks like a container signal but here tells you to tangle the letters of BEARCAT. The musical Cabaret grew from Christopher Isherwood's Berlin stories.
explanation.definitionFit: The stage musical, later a film, was adapted from Isherwood's Berlin novels via the play I Am a Camera.

clue.text: Theatrical agency beleaguered (concealing goddess)

indicators.note: the words in brackets are said to conceal something, so the answer is tucked inside the run of letters

explanation.surface: A theatrical agency is under siege, apparently with a goddess hiding among its staff.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across the end of 'agency' and the start of 'beleaguered'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cybele was the Phrygian mother goddess, worshipped in Greece and Rome as the Great Mother.

clue.text: One of William Goldman's titled relations

definitions.text: One of William Goldman's titled relations

parts.words: One of William Goldman's titled relations
parts.note: William Goldman wrote a novel whose title names a family relationship in the plural; one such sibling is wanted

explanation.surface: A question about a family member appearing in the title of a William Goldman book.
explanation.walkthrough: Goldman, author of Marathon Man, published the novel Brothers (1986), its sequel.
explanation.definitionFit: Goldman's novel title is the plural of this sibling word, so one of the titled relations is a single male sibling.

clue.text: Artist's trademark discerned in strange expression

indicators.note: something discerned in another thing is seen within it, so one piece goes inside the other
strange suggests the letters of the word for expression are made odd, that is rearranged

parts.note: an expression is a term, a word or phrase
a trademark is a brand name

explanation.surface: An artist's signature trait is spotted in an odd turn of phrase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' and 'discerned in' are the indicators; it is an indirect anagram, since the scrambled word is a synonym of 'expression', not printed. 'Artist's' is read as 'artist is'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dutch master painter of The Night Watch is a celebrated artist.

clue.text: Beatrice thought Benedick was a very valiant one S "Just one small step for man" like

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Beatrice thought Benedick was a very valiant one S "Just one small step for man" like': the OCR has run 5-down's clue into this one and no scan shows where it really ends.
annotationWithheld.clue: Beatrice thought Benedick was a very valiant one S "Just one small step for man" like

clue.text: A "retailer of state secrets at a low figure"

definitions.text: A "retailer of state secrets at a low figure"

parts.words: A "retailer of state secrets at a low figure"
parts.note: a quotation from The Mikado, where a corrupt official holding every great office of state offers to sell confidential information cheaply

explanation.surface: A quotation describing someone who sells off government secrets cheaply.
explanation.walkthrough: In Gilbert and Sullivan's The Mikado the Lord High Everything Else describes himself as a retailer of state secrets at a low figure.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gilbert and Sullivan character's name now means any self-important official holding many posts, and the quoted words are his own boast.

clue.text: "Just one small step for man" like

definitions.text: "Just one small step for man" like

parts.words: "Just one small step for man" like
parts.note: the moon-landing line suggests a single step, and the word wanted is the French and ballet term for one step

explanation.surface: A reference to Armstrong's line about a single step on the moon.
explanation.walkthrough: The French word for a step is also used in ballet, as in pas de deux.
explanation.definitionFit: In ballet and French the word means a single step, just what Armstrong's line describes.

clue.text: One among Horatio's rich friends?

indicators.note: among tells you the answer lies among the letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A guess about one of the wealthy acquaintances of Hamlet's friend Horatio.
explanation.walkthrough: The courtier sits inside 'Horatio's rich'. In Hamlet he is a foppish courtier whom Hamlet mocks for owning much fertile land, so he is rich; the question mark admits he is hardly a friend.
explanation.definitionFit: Osric is the affected, land-owning courtier in Hamlet who referees the final duel, so a wealthy figure in Horatio's circle.

clue.text: One from Islington had a daughter

definitions.text: One from Islington had a daughter

parts.words: One from Islington had a daughter
parts.note: refers to the old English ballad of a squire's son who loved a court officer's daughter living in Islington

explanation.surface: A remark about an Islington man and his daughter.
explanation.walkthrough: The ballad is The Bailiff's Daughter of Islington. Islington is a district of north London.
explanation.definitionFit: The ballad's title names this law officer as the father of the Islington girl.

clue.text: Characters like Walter Trevis's protagonist might be ruthless

indicators.note: might be tells you the letters of the next word could be rearranged into something else

explanation.surface: Figures modelled on a novelist's hero could well be merciless.
explanation.walkthrough: Walter Tevis (printed Trevis) wrote The Hustler, whose protagonist is the pool shark Fast Eddie Felson.
explanation.definitionFit: Tevis's protagonist is the title's pool sharp, so characters like him are con men of the same kind.

clue.text: Like neglected garden or Ulysses without Leopold

definitions.meaning: an untended garden has no flowers
Joyce's Ulysses follows Leopold Bloom; remove him and the book lacks its Bloom

explanation.surface: A neglected garden is compared to Joyce's novel stripped of its hero.
explanation.walkthrough: Leopold Bloom is the central character of Ulysses, so the novel without him is lacking Bloom.
explanation.definitionFit: A neglected garden has no flowers, and Ulysses minus Leopold has no Mr Bloom: both are without blossom or Bloom.

clue.text: Would Rose Macaulay have enjoyed this Brian Aldiss work?

definitions.text: Would Rose Macaulay have enjoyed this Brian Aldiss work?

parts.words: Would Rose Macaulay have enjoyed this Brian Aldiss work?
parts.note: Rose Macaulay wrote Pleasure of the title's subject, and Brian Aldiss wrote a novella of the same one-word title

explanation.surface: A question whether one novelist would have liked a book by another.
explanation.walkthrough: Macaulay's Pleasure of Ruins (1953) is about crumbling buildings; Aldiss published the novella Ruins (1987).
explanation.definitionFit: Macaulay wrote a whole book on the pleasure of ancient remains, and Aldiss's work bears that very word as title.

clue.text: Composer from Poole, hardly heard these days

indicators.note: from tells you the answer is taken out of the letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A composer from the Dorset town of Poole is seldom played nowadays.
explanation.walkthrough: The run straddles 'Poole' and 'hardly'; 'heard these days' only completes the surface. Poole is a town on England's south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Lehar was the Hungarian writer of operettas such as The Merry Widow.

clue.text: Tank war correspondent

definitions.meaning: the British infantry tank of the Second World War bore this name
the future prime minister reported on the Boer War for the Morning Post

explanation.surface: A tank and a journalist reporting from the front.
explanation.walkthrough: Winston Churchill was captured and escaped while reporting the Boer War; the tank was named after him.
explanation.definitionFit: The Second World War tank was named after the statesman, who as a young man reported from South Africa as a journalist.

clue.text: Blasé, unlike Gulley Jimson's Sara

definitions.meaning: Sara Monday, Gulley Jimson's model in Joyce Cary's novels, narrates Herself Surprised, so unlike her means not taken aback

explanation.surface: Someone is unimpressed, unlike a character from a Joyce Cary novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Joyce Cary's trilogy has Gulley Jimson (The Horse's Mouth) and Sara Monday, narrator of Herself Surprised.
explanation.definitionFit: A blasé person shows no astonishment, the opposite of Sara in the novel named Herself Surprised.

clue.text: Noble Dickensian "ugly and withered as one of the fantastic carvings… malignant as the Evil one

definitions.text: Noble Dickensian "ugly and withered as one of the fantastic carvings… malignant as the Evil one

parts.words: Noble Dickensian "ugly and withered as one of the fantastic carvings… malignant as the Evil one
parts.note: the quotation is from The Mystery of Edwin Drood, describing the old opium-den keeper with a royal nickname

explanation.surface: A Dickens character of rank is described in a quotation as hideous and wicked.
explanation.walkthrough: In Edwin Drood the opium seller in the London den is nicknamed Princess Puffer; 'Noble' plays on her title.
explanation.definitionFit: The opium-den woman of Edwin Drood is known by a royal title, so a noble figure in Dickens, and the quote describes her.

clue.text: Like ways beside the River Dove

definitions.text: Like ways beside the River Dove

parts.words: Like ways beside the River Dove
parts.note: recalls Wordsworth's Lucy poem, where she dwelt among unvisited ways beside the springs of Dove

explanation.surface: A description of paths running beside an English river.
explanation.walkthrough: Wordsworth's poem opens 'She dwelt among the untrodden ways / Beside the springs of Dove'.
explanation.definitionFit: Wordsworth calls the paths by the Dove unvisited by walkers, the word for paths no foot has worn.

clue.text: Arabian Nights-type weapon. To define it thus is it racism? perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the words before it are only one possible arrangement of the letters

explanation.surface: Describing a curved sword in Arabian Nights terms might be called racist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' marks the anagram of IT RACISM; the question mark plays on stereotyping in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The curved oriental sword is the blade associated with tales from the Arabian Nights.

clue.text: Noble Dickensian conversationalist?

parts.note: points to the titled foreign visitor in The Pickwick Papers who gathers garbled facts in conversation at Mrs Leo Hunter's party

explanation.surface: A question about a talkative aristocrat in Dickens.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Pickwick Papers the foreign Count Smorltork collects notes on England and mangles names; his surname hints at 'small talk'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pickwick count is titled, so noble, and his name sounds like small talk, making him a conversationalist.

clue.text: Like that prolific author who is a no-no in France

definitions.text: Like that prolific author who is a no-no in France

parts.words: Like that prolific author who is a no-no in France
parts.note: the prolific writer is Anon, who signs no name; the French touch hints at a word beginning with the French for one

explanation.surface: A joke about a busy writer who is unwelcome in France.
explanation.walkthrough: Anonymous is the most prolific author of all, and such a writer has no name given.
explanation.definitionFit: Anonymous works carry no given name, so their writer is without a name.

clue.text: Reported payment to rescue children's author

indicators.note: reported means spoken of, so the word for the payment is said out loud

parts.note: money paid to free a captive is a ransom

explanation.surface: News of money paid to save a writer of children's books.
explanation.walkthrough: Arthur Ransome wrote Swallows and Amazons.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Ransome is the author of the Swallows and Amazons books for young readers.

clue.text: St John Ervine made a play for his first wife

definitions.text: St John Ervine made a play for his first wife

parts.words: St John Ervine made a play for his first wife
parts.note: the playwright St John Ervine wrote a comedy titled after a man's former spouse

explanation.surface: A dramatist courts the woman who was his first wife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made a play for' seems to mean courted, but Ervine wrote the play The First Mrs Fraser (1929).
explanation.definitionFit: Ervine's comedy The First Mrs Fraser takes its title from the hero's former spouse.

clue.text: Greene's was quixotic

parts.note: Graham Greene wrote a novel about a Spanish priest named after Cervantes's knight

explanation.surface: A comment that something of Graham Greene's was idealistic.
explanation.walkthrough: Greene's novel is Monsignor Quixote (1982).
explanation.definitionFit: The cleric's title in Greene's Monsignor Quixote precedes Quixote, so his rank was literally quixotic.

clue.text: Very small unit in charge of order in Greece

parts.note: an ion is a tiny charged particle

explanation.surface: A tiny team in command keeps discipline in Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'order' is a classical order of architecture, not discipline.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ionic is one of the classical orders of architecture, with scroll-shaped capitals, from ancient Greece.

clue.text: St Clare was Tom's

parts.note: in Uncle Tom's Cabin Augustine St Clare buys Tom and so holds him as property

explanation.surface: A statement that someone called St Clare belonged to Tom.
explanation.walkthrough: In Harriet Beecher Stowe's novel the relation runs the other way: St Clare was Tom's master.
explanation.definitionFit: St Clare purchased Tom in Uncle Tom's Cabin, so he was the slave's possessor.

clue.text: I'm not to be confused with Lucian's misanthrope

indicators.note: to be confused means to be muddled up, so the letters before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone insists they must not be mistaken for a famous hater of mankind.
explanation.walkthrough: Lucian's dialogue Timon, or the Misanthrope, also inspired Shakespeare's play.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucian wrote a satirical dialogue about the Athenian Timon, the man-hater.

clue.text: "The silent fisher casts th' —— food" (Pope)

parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank from Pope's Windsor Forest, where the angler's bait is described as treacherous

explanation.surface: A line from Pope about an angler with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The word wanted describes the bait as sly and treacherous.
explanation.definitionFit: The angler's bait deceives the fish, so Pope calls it treacherous food.

clue.text: How T. H. White's knight was made

definitions.text: How T. H. White's knight was made

parts.words: How T. H. White's knight was made
parts.note: T. H. White's book about Lancelot is titled for a badly formed knight

explanation.surface: A question about how a knight in a T. H. White book was created.
explanation.walkthrough: The third part of The Once and Future King is The Ill-Made Knight, about Lancelot.
explanation.definitionFit: White's Lancelot volume is The Ill-Made Knight, so the knight was badly made.

clue.text: Tom Wolfe's fundamental chic?

parts.note: Tom Wolfe's essay mocked society hosts courting the Black Panthers, and the missing word also means fundamental

explanation.surface: A question about Tom Wolfe's basic sense of style.
explanation.walkthrough: Wolfe's 1970 essay is Radical Chic; the word also means going to the root.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means going to the root, hence fundamental, and it completes the title of Wolfe's essay with chic.

clue.text: Chaucer, with devious ruse, introduces Nijinsky, for example

parts.note: Spenser called Chaucer 'Dan Chaucer', Dan being an old title of respect like Master

indicators.note: devious means departing from the straight path, so the letters of ruse are moved off course

explanation.surface: Chaucer, using a sly trick, presents the great Russian dancer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'devious' is the anagram indicator. Spenser called Chaucer 'Dan Chaucer', Dan being an old honorific; 'introduces' only links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Vaslav Nijinsky was a celebrated male ballet dancer of the Ballets Russes.
